¥S am particularly happy to go through the manuscript of Shri Subrata Kumar Banerjea's Synoptic Memorizer of
Materia Medica. The reason for this is that | have not come across someone himself a student of the College who has put in such diligence and produced a worth-while book. Having himself gone through the mill recen

known the difficulties of his colleagues, he has particularly
written it for their benefit as its name suggests. However,
1 feel that even those in the profession would considerably
profit from its study. So far, he has;covered only fifty
remedies and | do hope that he will bring out further
volumes to cover the rest of the Materia Medica.
A mere glance at the different headings and the
chapters gives an insight into his vast study and great
labour in writting this book.
There fas often been a debate as to whether the
Materia Medica should give the personality profiles or the key-notes. From the name of the bodék. one may be inclined to put it in the latter category. However, looking through it, one finds a blend of both as some explanation or details of the outstanding symptoms are mentioned with many of the remedies.
The Repertorial references and the Comparative Materia
Medica, so essential for an accurate prescribing, are very welcome aspects of this book.
There are many Materia Medicas that are available and the question can be asked is there need for more? My answer is that every author looks at the gem of our remedies from a different angle and sheds a new lIustre by bringing ‘out some fresh points or at least arranging it in a new form.
As mentioned above, it would be particularly welcomed by the students of the homoeopathic institutions especially when they are preparing for their examinations.

Co write a new Materia Medica is a greatest absurdity,—it can only be delineated in a new approach and illustration, to reiterate in a novel fashion, to cope with the needs. Thus with this book also,—it is a synopsis of different views and styles of presentation of drug-pictures as adopted by our immortal Master Samuel Hahnemann, our delightful Kent, iamented Hering, erudite Dunham, sagacious Clarke, discreetful Nash- prudent Allen etc. etc.
| have liberally taken references from their classic literatures, with a view to generate enthusiasm and to arouse the latent curiosity of the young homoeopathiec generations in those treasure references,—the store-house of knowledge, as they are really our precious wealth. For this reason ! have mentioned their good-names, whenever their views has been expressed.
Throughout the book, reader may note that repeatedly
{ have obliged to mention, ‘Master Kent’—adoptation of this style has néver intended to demote the honour of that prodigious personality, the versatile genius, our imperishable
Master Samuel Hahnemann, but only to impress the readers and above all to generate interest and curiosity in Kent’s literatures; as it is perhaps only ‘Master Kent’ who can delineate and depict the drug-picture in our mind in a lucid comprehensible fashion; besides this he is regarded as ‘Master’ by many renowned authorities throughout the globe for his masterly dedication of many classic literatures to the homoeopathic fraternity.
The appearance of this book has never intended to
Jeplace the text-books or our wealthy literatures, but only

to imprint the drug-pictures in the faculty of intutiqn in a more comprehensible fashion. Hence | have adopted my own technique to enumerate every drug-picture and mental-picture in such a comprehensible fashion so that they can be memorized easily such as, know the medicine through the name of the medicine or through any suitable denotative connotation, viz. Sulphur through the word Philosopher,
Thuja through the tips Sycosis, Bryonia through the tips
Modality etc. etc. This expedient of memorizing our vast
Materia Medica is entirely designed by me and thus I am presenting this artistic style before the homoeopathic fraternity. | think this fashion of memorizing our vast Materia
Medica will serve some beneficial purpose, espcially for the examinees, as well as those. are in the profession.

The heart-felt desire of many of my coaching students, and above all my dearest parents’, my Bara-Ma’s and many of my friends inspiration has set my heart on taking this venture.
The major part of this book was originally my personal notes, but for this purpose they have been thoroughly designed and profusely augmented. The mental pictures and the drug-pictures are some-what voluminous, at least from the examination point of view : but my actual intention is to depict the picture in a broad and elaborated fashion, elucidating different views from different angles, for quick and vivid comprehension ;—to make the gist. will not be of problem, provided they grasp the thought.

On coming to an end, | must commemorate the sacred memory of my past homoeopathic generations—my homoeopathic ancestors, those have descended me the ‘true haemoeopathic blood’—perhaps the rooct-cause of my deepest regard ia this ‘divine art of healing’.
{ must acknowledge with honour the names of my revered professors,—Dr. P. C. Paul, Dr. S. K. Dubey,
Dr. Sripati Mandal, Dr. T. P. Mandal, Dr. S. R. Saha,
Dr. M. M. Dutta, Dr. Mahendra Singh, Dr. Gopal Mukherjee,
Dr. N. K. Mitra, Dr. S. C. Ghosh, Dr. D. Tarafdar, Dr. H. P.
Saha. Dr. K. N. Chakraverty. Dr. J. Barman, Dr. B. Santra,

and Dr. Ashit Banerjee, those have encountered their best possible endeavour in teaching me this ‘rational art’, and my all success is due t0 them and to be conferred upon them as their success ; my gratitlide to them.
| must convey my sincere regards and gratitude to my dearest parents, as they are my constant source of inspira-tion and my beloved ‘Bara-Ma’, whom | endearingly revere and her dedication is ineffable. Their immense love was the only key to my success.
Last but not the least, {am obliged to mention the names of Kajal Bhattacharyya, Satyajeet Sinha, Debabrata
Sarkar, Akhilesh Khan, Swapan Paria, Samir Pyne and
Madhumeeta Mitra, as their constant inspiration, un-stining help and co-operation, un-ending patience in every regard has made this effort possible, yet | can not narrow down our relation by mere thanking them, as such a relation does not exists amongst us,—our relation is above such courtesy.
Lastly, | am frankly inviting afl sorts of constructive suggestions and this is to confess that if this book can win the heart of the readers, thence that will be my finest yeward.

Subrata Kumar Banerjea.

in the physical sphere it is evidenced as slight bearable pain to her becomes unbearable she jumps in agony, a
State of hyperaesthesia. Dr. Hering said due to this mental anxiety he is agonized and tossing about.
Note : Fear of future and forebodings also charac-terizes this anxiety li) Calmness contraindicates Aconite :
Dr. Guernsey said, “Mental ca/mness contraindicates
Aconite. (Chamo.— indicates, Puls ).
Thus whenever Aconite will be the drug of choice, there must be the mentaf uneasiness, mental restlessness, worry, anx/ety and great fear, otherwise it is contraindicated

iil) Overwhelming fear :
It is one of our leading remedy having different charac-teristic types of fear.
it has) got not that type of fear viz., fear of poverty like. Bryonia. fear of thunder like Phos.; fear of dogs like Bell.; fear of approach like Arnica. fear of being alone like Ars,
Arg Nit.; but it has got that characteristic fear, that is fear of death with prediction of day and time of death.
Dr. Tyler said, fear of death may be so _ great, that people have actually killed themseives for fear of dying.
Hence Aconite.* has got fear of death (Ars.!, Calc. Carb.?,
Cimicifuga’, Gels.*, Lac Can.1, Nit. Ac.*, Phos.?, Platina‘) (Ref.
Kent's Repertory) but the characteristic is pt. predicts the day; even the time of death, i. e., the clairvoyance. Master Kent sald, many times the pt actually predicts the moment or hour of death: if a clock is in the pt.‘s room, she may say, that when the hour hand reaches a certain point, she will be a corpse. Dr. Tyler said. i is Aconite pt. who calls her friends around her and takes leave of them. Foar
of death

chapters.content:
is such an important feature. Dr. Farrington said that prediction of hour of the death esp. in childbed is also found in it and can be bracketed with Argentum Nit. and Coffea.
Besides this : (a) fear of darkness ( Can. Ind.*, Strarmo.?, Acon.?, Calc. C.?,
Camph.?, Carb. An.?, Carb. Veg.*, Caust.?, Cup.?, Lyco 2,
Phos.?, Puls.?. )
{b) fear of bed ( Acon.*, Ars.*, Caust.*, Cup.*, Lach.” }
(c) fear of ghost ( Acon.*, Ars.?, C.V.*, Caust.?, Lyco.*,
Phos.?, Puls.%, Sulph.? )
{d) fear of going out, fear of crawd ( Acon.”, Arg. N.?,
Lyco.?, Nat. Mur *, Nux Vom 2, Puls.® ).
Note : Dr. Nash said, ‘fear to go into society’"—
Anthrapophabia.
{e) fear of death in pregnancy (Acon.*). (f) fear of approaching death (Arg. Nit., Ars , Cimic., Nit. Ac.,
Secale Cor.) (Ref. Cowperthwaite). (g) fears the loss of reason—leading to mental prostration with
weakness of memory, can not remember dates. (Ref.
Dr Talcatt’s Mental diseases).

iv) Nash’s trio of restless :
Aconite is one of the Nash's trio of restless medicines.
Aconite is mentally restless, where as Rhus Tox. is physically restless and Arsenic is restless both mentally and physically thus the trio ; Acon., Ars. Alb., and Rhus Tox.
Dr, E. B. Nash said, fear, as much as the pain that makes‘
the pt. so full of that agonized restlessness.
Dr. N. M. Chowdhury said, the impatience and anxiety makes the pt. restiess. She throws herself about and cons-tantly changes the position. The true reason of this restless-ness is to be found in a state of internal turmoil and anxiety and agony. She moans and laments, screams and shouts, not knowing what to do and how to find consolation.
In such a case of mental restlessness, Aconite will be the drug of cholse ;—give her drug— it will] cure.

4 Synoptic Memerizer of Materia Medica

v) iIgnatia like hysterical :
Aconite patient is also inclined to be hysterical. (Caust.!,
Gels.*, Ign.?, Lach.2, Nat Mur.*, Nit. Ac.7, Nux Vom.*, Puis.?,
Sep.*, Sil.4) Dr N. M. Chowdhury said, great variation of
Mood and temperament. She is cheerful this minute, weeps
the next. She is sad and taciturn now but gay and
foquacious the next moment.
Master Kent said, sometimes Acontte pt. looses all her
affection, which leads to a state of indifference—this state
is also characterized by Aysterical mood.
Dr. Talcott said pt. moves from dry anyuish to exuberant
tears.
vi) Tension is the key-note :
Dr. Huge said, tension is the key note of Aconite pt.
( —Congestion is the keynote of Belli. ).
This tension is mentally evidence by intense restlessness,
inconsolable anxiety, acute imagination and fears. vii) Uncommon peculiar sensations :
It has got some peculiar sensations. viz.,
a) All the intellectual functions are going on in the region of the stomach.
b) Some parts of the body is deformed e.g., a limb is displaced, fips are too thick. ( Ref. Farrington ). viii) Music makes her sad :
Music is unbearable for Aconite pt.; it makes her sad ( Acon.?, Graph.*, Dig.*, Kreos.*, Nat.C.*, Thuja.?,) ( —music > Aurum.”, Tarent.? ).
Note. 1 :
Countenance :
Master Kent has pointed to note the countenance of
Aconite, which is expressive of fear. Fear is depicted upon her countenance.
Note. 2:
Dr. Kent reported that every mental condition ig marked by intensity. If it is a delirium, thence it is intense ; ——thus

MENTAL PICTURES 5

Dr. Farrington said the intensity of these symptoms denotes overexcitement of brain, common enough to hysterical patients.
Note. 3:
Master Kent said, this type of mental picture is always present in pneumonia, inflammatory conditions of any part, or kidney, liver, bowels etc.
Note. 4 :
In case of females amenorrhoea in plethoric young girls after fright is a marked feature.
Note. 5 :
Our immortal Master Hahnemann said ‘whenever Aconite is chosen homoasopathically, you must above all, observe the moral symptoms, and be careful that it cioselfy resembles them ; the anguish of mind and body: the restlessness; the disquiet not to be allayed’
Note. 6:
Master Kent said even congestion of parts as a result of fear. A turmoil affecting the whole sensorium. iv) Modality :
Mental symptoms < in the evening, towards night.

a) Bad effects of disappointment of love ( Hyos.*,

Staph.*, Caust.?, Nux. Vom.*). ( —love sick, Ant.C.*; —love with sifent grief, [gn.*, Nat. Mur.*, Phos Ac.*).
1. Character :
i) Angry child :
Ant. Crud. is a medicines suits for extremes of life ( Verat.
Alb. }—affecting child and aged. Hence Ant. Crud. child bears a pecullar mentality.
it can be compared with the race of swine for the virtue of the fact that it inclines to grow Zet and mecreover its typical obstinacy.
The chifdis angry and obstinate, fretful, peevish, can’t bear to be touched or to be looked at, sulky, does not wish to speak or be Spoken to ( Ant Tart.; lod.; Sil.). Angry at every little attention.
Becomes angry at silly matters, il-humour characterizes the angry chiid.
Note. 1: Dr. Farrington said this peevish mental state is
associated with nausea, hot and red face and irregular pulse.
Note. 2: Dr. Farrington said the child is particularly cross
when washed in cold water. iit) No desire to live :
itis tiger prescriber Tyler Kent who has elucidated the picture.
Master Kent said, it produces a very serious state of mind, an absence of the desire to live. Pt. says, ‘Oh. doctor, if i could only die’—such an aversion, loathing of life is confined to Ant. Crud. pt.
Note. 1: Master Kent said this state is especially found in a low, lingering, continued fever such as typhoid. Such a typhoid will sometimes be seen in young giris about puberty, who are threatening to go into chlorosis. They have loathing of life, but it is a Aysterical loathing of life
Note. 2: Dr. Henry Clarke said disgust of life, with an incli-nation to blow one’s brain out, to drown oneself. Great anxiety about his fate and inclination to shoot himself.

MENTAL PICTURES 7

iii) Timidity :
Timidity is another feature. The pt is timid, morose and there is graat sadness berne in the mind
Dr. Farrington said pt. is sulky and sad like Puls. iv) trresistable desire to talk in rhymes :
There is an /srresistable desira to talk in poem whichis common enough to hysterical women. v) Moonlight <. :
Over-sxcitable, nervous, hysterical, ecstatic young girls and women are overcome by moeilow-light from the moon—and there is ‘sentimental mood especially in the moonlight’
( Ref. Kent ).
Master Kent said, it ts a hysterical state, a disorderly outburst of the affections, which especially aggravated in the moon-light.
Note. 1 :
Dr N. M. Chowdhury said Ant C. is moon-struck.
Note. 2 :
Dr Farrington said in some cases there is a erotic condition of mind, connected with sexual erethism. vi) Commit suicide by drowning :
Ant Crud pt wants to commit suicide by drowning ( Bell ?, Hell.*, Hyos.*, Lach?®, Puls °, Rhus Tox.*) ( —by hanging, Ars.?,—with knife, Ars?, Calc C*, Merc? ; —by shooting, Ant. C.? vii) Repeat verses :
This is a marked peculiarity that Ant. Crud opt. like to talk in verses. Pt. also repeat verses esp in the moonlight. vili) Unsatisfied :
Dr. John Henry Clarke satd pt. is not satisfied though whatever is done for him This ts a peculiar mentality borne in Ant. C. pt.
Dr. N. M. Chowdhury also said that the baby whines and cries and nothing pleases him.
Dr. Talcott reported in his book ‘Mental diseases’ —that has amorous longings, not for any living creature, but for some unseen seraph boded forth by an ecstatic imagination

S Synoptic Memorizer of Materia Medica

ix) Dull :
Dr. Clarke reported that Ant. Crud pt. is dull. Dutiness of
intellect, imbecility.
Hil. Modality :
< in open fire (Kent said, open fire is wholly against the
Ant Crud. pt.) ; < in moon-light.
Note. : Dr. Talcott said it is suited to the mental condition of
some young persons passing through the critical pubescent
period, whose growing interest in the opposite sex tends to
center unhealthfully.

Q. Elucidate the mental picture of ARGENTUM NITRICUM.
1 like to impress you the entire mental picture through the word—-ARGENTUM.
A= Apprehension, anxious.
R=Reserved, sad.
G=Great haste.
E= Excitable, easily angered.
N= Notions, Nervous, Neglected.
T=Tendency to suicide.
U= Undue fear of projecting buildings.
M= Memory loss.
1. Mental Causations :
1) Apprehension.
ii) Fear.
iii) Mental stress and strain.
iv) Acute or chronic diseases from unusual or jong-continued mental exertion.
v) Symptoms comes on as a result of his anxiety (Kent).
vi) Dr. Talcott said mental symptoms results from over-indulging in the use of alcohol and excess in venery.
Il. Character :
a) Apprehension and anxiety : There is a great
apprehension which Master Kent in his voluminous Repertory kept in the subrubric: anxiety, anticipating an engagement (Arg. N.*, Gels.*, Medo.?).
Anxiety and apprehension when getting ready to go to ch urch, opers, examination, or any other engagement and at

MENTAL PICTURES 9

that diarrhoea sets in 1. e., apprehensive d/arrhoea (Gels.).
Dr. Tyler said, it is one of the great remedy of examination funk (Aethusa., Gel., Kali Phos., Anac.)
Dr. Tyler said, pt. breaks into sweat with anxiety when
‘going to a wedding, to church, to opera.
b) Reserved : _.
Our Arg. Nit. pt. is reserved, introvert in their disposition.
Pt. is sad taciturn, gloomy.
Dr. Farrington said in some cases we find profoud melancholy.
c) Great haste :
The pt. is very much /mpulsive, does everything in a great haste, even eats and drinks in a great haste, must walk fast.
Dr. Farrington said pt. seems to be always busy yet accomplishes nothing. He hurries restlessly to fulfill an engagement, thinking that he will be too late, hence does everything in a great haste.
In Dr. Kents’ Repertory it has been placed to the sub-rubric
—hurry to arrive for the appointed time. (Arg Nit.*) -—hurry while walking (Arg Nit.*, Sulph Ac.*, Tarent.*, Sulph.?,
Thuja.?),—hence time passes too slowly ( Can Ind.*, Glon.*,
Alumina.?, Arg. N.2, Medo.?, Merc.2, Nux Mos.*, Nux Vom.? )
— too quickly, (‘ Cocc.*, Therid.*),
da) Excitable :
Arg Nit. pt. are easily excitable, easily angered — which brings on pain in head and chest.
6) Notions :
Strange notions crowded in Arg Nit. pt.
Master Kent said, dread of crowd.
Pt. has a strange notion that some serious incurable disease has overtaken him, imagines that if he left afone, he will die. Dr. Farrington said apprehension of some incurable diseases of brain.
Builds casties in air in the day and sees monstrous visions at night.

10 Synoptic Memorizer of..Mlateria Medica

Dr. Talcott in his Book ‘Mental disease reported that Arg
Nit. pt. hesitates to undertake anything from the fear of failure ( Arnica. ).
Arg. Nit. also possesa strange notion that he has been neglected and despised by everybody and thus finds no pleasure in his Iife.
Dr. Tyler said that Arg Nit. has also c/austrophobia —\ e., fear of confinement, which is a strange notion [t has also got anthropophobia { Acon.’, Arg N* Aur.*, Nat. Mur.?
N.V ®, Puls.?}) and dreads certain places.
f) Tendency to suicide :
Suicidal tendency prevails upon the pt. when crossing through high altitudes, bridge etc. On looking down from high altitude creates a peculiar type of /mpulses to jump out of the place Master Kent tn his Repertory classed it in the sub-rubric—throwing himself from a height (Aur.?, Arg N.?,
Vell.*, N.V.?).
Master Kent reported fear of death, often predicts the moment of death.
g) Undue fear of projecting buildings :
Arg Nit. pt. has great fear of projecting buildings and corners which creates a sensation as if it would fall over him
The sight of the projecting buildings makes the pt. d/zzy
Dr. Farrington has remarked about this fear of projecting buildings and corners that it is due to the m/stake of esti-mation of distances ie., derangement of the sense, derange-ment of the sense of distance, depth and magnitude — altitude sense derangement, so that the pt. thinks that he will run against those and have a clash.
Dr Tyler said even in the street the s/ght of high houses always made him giddy and caused him to stagger. It seem as if the houses on both sides would approach and crush him.
Dr. N. M. Chowdhury reported that this altitude sense derangement is due to imperfect co-ordination of occular muscles.
h) Memory Loss :
There is frequent loss of memory, makes frequent fault in

MENTAL PICTURES 1t

speech, because he can not find right word during conver-sation.
Master Kent said, disturbance in the memory. Irrational in his explanations of his actions and methods.

| like to depict the mental picture of Aurum Metallicum through the name of the remedy.
A=Anxlous abuut future.
U=Unpardonable crime and sins.
R=Realisation of them.
U=Unwanted element.
M-- Melancholia

1. Mental causations :
i) Grief.
ii ) Disappointed love
iii) Reserved displeasure, unfulfilled fongings ( Ref. N. M.
Chowdhury ).
iv) Vexation, mortification.
v) Fear, fright.
vi) Contradiction.
vii) Mercurial and syphilitic bad-effect.
Note : Syphilitic miasm engrafted on scrofulous base.
ll. Character :
i) Anxious about future :
Our typical Aurum. pt. is anxious about the future ( Bry.",
C.C.1, Phos.? ). Master Kent said, future looks dark to him
looks on the dark side of everything.

12 Synoptic Memorizer of Materia Medica

ii ) Unpardonable crime and sins :
He feels as if he had commited many unpardonable crimes and sins when he was young. Master Kent said, as if, he is. wholly evil. iii) Realisation of them :
On realisation of those crimes, he repents. Master Kent said, pt. broods over it but that hatches new grievances, and intensifies the symptom. He is eager to redemption of those crimes and sins, those he has commited since youth.
Master Kent said, pt. thinks that he has neglected some-thing. Reproach of neg/ected duty. We deserves reproach in consequence of having neglected duty — is not worthy of salvation. iv) Unwanted element :
As the pt. broods — that makes the pt. to think that he is an unwanted element in the society. He feels that life is
@ constant burden to him. v) Melancholia :
Dr. Farrington said in almost ail cases in which it is simi-limum, there is present of melancholy with disposition to weep or with a feeling of self-condemnation.
Dr. N. M. Chowdhury reported that most important characteristic is profound melancholia ( Aur.1, C.C.1, Caust.?,
Graph.?, Gels.*, Ign.?, Nat Mur.?, Puls.? ).
Pt. is sad, despondent, dejested, with jnvo/untary weeping
C Ign.7, Nat Mur.?, Plat.?, Puls.7, R. Tox.?, Sep 7, Aur.?, Bell.*,
Caust.* ), apathetic with complete d/sgust of Ife. Dr. Kent said suitable in most profound states of melancholia, —pt. sits and says nothing. Melancholy, feels shateful and quarre/some.
Dr. Taicott recommended that sometimes we find religious melancholia whence constant prayer is noticable.
Master Kent said, absolute loss of enjoyment in everything.
Constantly expecting bad news, the future looks dark to him
— resulting melancholia.
Note : Master Kent said, Aurum. state of mind is an insanity,

MENTAL PICTURES 13

dreadful to look upon because of !ts turbulence and melan-choly Terrible melancholy after mercury vt) Miserable life :
Life is a constant burden to him, hence to get rid of it, he constantly dwelis on suicide ( Naja., Nat. S ,— but is afraid to die, Nux Vom. ). Dr. Farrington said, pt. has suicidal thoughts, even if pt. does not make actual attempts to suicide
Dr. Boericke said constantly dwelling on suicide yet fear of death.
Dr. E. B. Nash said, in men, it is oftenest in connection with liver troubles : in women with womb troubles esp. when enlarged, endurated or prolapsed.
Master Kent said affections are natural to healthy men—-
but these are perverted. Love Of living, of self protection, is perverted—longs to die, seeks methods to commit suiside
He mediates upon death, upon suicide. He wants to get out of the world. vii) Excessive questioning :
Dr. Boericke said, excessive questioning without waiting for reply is another feature of Aur. Met. vii) Tremendous Oversensitive :
Our Aurum Met. is exceedingly oversens/tive, a mere noise in the door makes the pt. anxious. ix) Aggravations & Ameliorations :
< from sunset to sun rise.
< from mental exertion.
< from melancholic brooding.
> in the morning ( Clarke ). x) Low-sspirited :
Arum Met. pt. is tife-less, pt. feels uneasy, has great desire for mental and physical activity but can’t do things fast enough xi) Life-Less :
it seems that joyousness of mind is not for Aurum Met.
He is melancholic, depressed, excessive scruples of conscience. There is aversion to conversation. Dr. Kent said,

14 Synoptic Memorizer of Materia Medica

he wants to destroy himself, has no love for his life which he thinks worthless. xii) Inferiority Complex ;
inferiority complex (— superiority complex, Platina ), is a grand feature of this medicine.
Self condemnation is inborn, there is depressive insanity (+++), hence pt. broods and inferiority complex becomes evidently marked.
Master Kent classically explained that continual self-reproach, self-criticism, imagines he can’t succeed in anything and he does everything wrong—he is in dis-union with himself. Imagines he sees obstacles in this way everywhere xiii) Contradiction unbearable :
Least contradiction excites his wrath (Nash), contradic-tion is unbearable (Aur.', Ign.1, Lyco.1, Sep.1, Bry.?, Coce.?,
N. V.?, Sil.?}}makes him irritable and excites him. Master
Kent said, every little thing rouses him into anger and turmoil.
Dr. Farrington said any contradiction or dispute excitie$ the patient furiously, he becomes red in face and his pugnacity is aroused. xiv) Unhappy :
Master Kent gave the picture. Sometimes he is sound in his business affairs, seems to be an intelligent man but silently broods over his state and is hatred of the world, tells nohody of it, thus he becomes unhappy, and thence found being hang in his room.
Q. The mental picture of ARSENICUM ALBUM.
{ like to impress the mental picture of Arsenic through the word ‘Fastidious’, as Arsenic. is very fastidious; thus remember the mental! picture through this word.
F=— Fear.
A= Anxious.
S= Sad.
T= Time modality.
t=Incurable disease.

{== Irritable.
O= Orderly mania.

i) Grief (Ref. Clarke).
ii) Fright (Ref. Clarke).
iii) Fit of passion
iv) Long exposure to malarial influences. ij. Characters :
a) Fear:
Arsenic pt. has feer of death. Master Kent said, dread of death when alone, or on going to bed. He thinks that he ts going to die and wants somebody with him.
Master Kent reported that a sudden anxious fear comes over him at night, he jumps out of bed with fear that he is going to die, or that,he is going to suffocate. Sometimes fear drives him out of bed, he hides in a closet.
Dr. J. H. Clarke said: i) fear of solitude,
ii) fear of spectres,
iii} morbid fear of cholera (Nit. Ac ),
iv) fear of robbers ( Ars.?, Arg. N.?,
Ign.*, Lach.*, Merc.*, Nat M.?, Phos 2)
Note : Master Kent said, he has violent increase of his fear and horror in the dark and many complaints come on im the evening as darkness is coming on. b) Anxious :
Master Kent said, t#e anxfety that is found in Arsenic. 7s intermingled with fear.
The anxiety takes form also in the restlessness ( it is restless both mentally and physically, one of the member of
Mash’‘s trio of restless medicines).
This anxious restlessness has three phases.
in acute stage, pt. goes from chair to chair, child goes from nurse to mother, from one’s lap to other.
Thence an uneasiness comes as this constant change of

16 Synoptic Memorizer of Materia Medica

position makes the patient exhaustsd. Thence he is in bed and
unable to sit up, thus rolis in bed and thence the prostration
comes out of position. Exhaustion is not felt while lying still,
but as soon as he moves, pt is surprised to find himself so weak. Thus this leads to cadaveric aspect of the pt, when he lies in bed hke a cadaver
Thus Master Kent warns us to remember that these state
of anxiety and restlessness go towards the cadaveric aspect, towards death. Kent said, at first there is that anxious rest-lessness with fear, but the increasing weakness tends towards prostration.
Master Kent also reported another phase of anxiety viz anxiety like one who has commited murder. He finally works up to the idea that the officers are coming after him and watches if they are coming in to arrest him
Some unusual evil is going to happen — hence he is anxious.
Extreme anxiety in the evening in bed, said Master Kent c) Sad:
Sadness- prevails to a great extreme Master Kent said, averse to meeting — because he imagines that he has formerly offended them. Great menta/ depression, great sadness, melancholy with despair of recovery. Pt. is so sad that he is weary of life ; he loathes life and wants to die.
Dr. Clarke said that great apathy and indifference also characterizes Ars. Alb.
Dr. N. M. Chowdhury said very frequently the insanity takes the form of religious melancholia characterized by hopelessness and despairs of his salvation, life holds out no charm for him—melancholia. d) Time modality :
Master Kent reported that many of the mental! troubles ( as well as physical troubles ), come on and increased at certain times < from 1-2 P. M. and 1-2 A. M. < after midnight, very soon after midnight his sufferings begins and
1—2 O'clock they are intensified.

MENTAL PICTURES 17

e) Incurable disease :
Pt. thinks that his disease is incurable — his disease is
fatal and # is useless to take medicine as he is surely going
to die.
f) Dreads solitude : ;
Ars. Alb. pt. dreads solitude. Aversion to being alone
( Kali C., Bis., Lyco ) ( —Rev., Ign., Nux Vom. ).
Master Kent said, pt. dreads solitude and wants company,
because in company he can talk and put off the fear.
Dr. Talcott said, fears to be left alone lest he should do
himself bodily harm.
g) Irritable :
Irritability is also a feature of Ars. Alb. Master Kent in
his repertory kept it in the second grade. Though Kent kept
it in first grade in the rubric, ailments after anger with anxiety
(Acon.?, Ign.?, Nux Vom.?).
h) Orderly mania :
A morbid fastidjousness has its similimum in Arsenic ( Ref.
Tyler ).
Pt. keeps everything in order,—tip-top. These patients
are hard to please.
Dr. C. Hering is justified in calling Ars Alb. pt as
“A gold-headed cane patient’. i) Un-natural Oversensitive :
Sensitiveness is a feature of Arsenic. Oversensitive to circumstances, to surroundings of the room_ characterizes
Ars. Alb. (Ref. Tyler). j) Suicidal tendency :
Kent reported, Ars pt. does commit suicide It is a remedy full of suicidal tendencies Suicidal dispositioh esp. at night and after midnight (Nux Vom ) ( Ref. Kents’ Repertory ).
Suicidal disposition by hanging ( Bell.?, Nat. Sulph *), with knife (Calc Carb.*, Merc *)
Dr N. M. Chowdhury said, as the pt. despairs of his salvation, life holds out no charm for him — this disgust for life is manifested by great anguish and restlessness and he tries to kill himself esp. by hanging (— Dr. N. M. Chowdhury

18 Synoptic Memorizer of Materia Medica

compared this suicidal tendency with Aurum Met, a_ sove-reign remedy for insanity with suicidal ideas by shooting or
throwing himself from a height, engrafted in a syphilitic or
syphilo-mercurial constitution ; — Ant Crud does miracles
in sentimental insanity, people who are moon-struck and love-Sick, wants to end their miseries by shooting or drowning)
Note 1: Dr J. H. Clarke compares Ars Alb with the race of
horse, as this animal typifies As. Alb. temperament. The hors "
is exceedingly nervous animal, constantly moving about, rest-less to a degree and very prone to take fright —quite a
picture of the Arsenic temperament
Note 2: According to Dr Teste Ars. Alb. acts more power-fully on vegetarians. (—Rev, Nux Vom., Allium Sativa).

_Q __Enumerate the mental picture of BELLADONNA.
! like to impress the total mental picture of BELLADONNA
through the word ‘DELIRIUM’

=—Excessive oversensitive.

I. Mental causations :
Regarding mental causations no definite stamping can be
made, yet Master Kent said plethoric, vigorous, intellectual or
brainy people have complaints suddenly.
li. Character :
a) Delusion :
In our Bell. pt. we find various forms of strange delusion,
Mlusion and hallucination,
Master Kent said, those are delightful to study but dread-ful to look-upon. Throughout the acute mania and through-out the delirious state, all the manifestations partake of violence.

MENTAL PICTURES 19

Pt imagines that he sees ghost, hideous faces, various
insects ( Ars.*, Bell.*, Lac C.?, Stramo.? ); dogs ( Bell.*, Aeth 4
Calc C.*, Stramo.*); wolves (Bell.?, Stramo ? ) ; phantoms
( Bell.1, Lach.?, Apis.*, Arg N.?, Ars.?, C.V.2, Hep.*, Hyos.?,
Lyco.*, Merc.*, Nat Mur.?, Phos.?, Thuja.?).
Master Kent in his Repertory classed Belladonna in first
grade in the subrubric that delusion on closing the eyes
(Bell.*, Calc C.?, Arg N.?, Bry.?, Op.?, Tarent. 2).

This is a strong point of correspondence with syphilis.
Note 1: It is esp. noticeable in the bone pains.
Note 2 . Merc. is Hahnemann’'s typical antisyphilitic remedy,
as Sulph, is the typical antipsoric and Thuja, the typical
antisycotic. But by this, it does not mean that they do not
cover the other miasms, as for example, Dr. J. H. Clarke said,
‘Merc. has relation to psora and sycosis as well as syphilis.’

GUIDING SYMPTOMS 103

2. Every little injury suppurates :
Hep., Sil, Graph, Petrol, Sulph. — afl has this symptom.
There is a suppurative tendency viz formation of ulcer.
Suppuration of the lungs after pneumonic haemorrhages (KaliC), glandular swellings with or without suppuration but esp, If suppuration be too profuse Cold swellings - abscesses, slow to suppurate
Dr. Clarke reports, Merc. intensifies the action of the absor-bents, it may also paralysis them, hence enlargement of glands, with pricking pains, inflammation, suppuration.
Dr. Kent reports that marked feature of Merc is the ten-dency to formation of the pus with inflammation, there is burning and stinging and the rapid formation of pus and the part is <. by both heat and cold.
3. Rt.-sided affection :
Dr. Clarke said the hver has been the chief excuse for
Mercurialism in the past and Merc. certainly has a powerful liver action. The liver ts congested, enlarged, inflarmmed, stitches in the liver, sens:tiveness in the liver and /nab/lity to fie on right side. This “< lying on right side “should always be considered.
4. Chilly ".
Dr. Nash discussed and amplified that the chill of
Merc. is peculiar. It is nota shaking chill, but is simply a
*‘creeping chilliness’’. (—Gels. big chills with heavy limbs ;
—chills from every movement, from leaving the fire, Nux Vom.).
*-Often when this creeping chilliness ts felt, it is the first symp tom of a cold that has been taken and if left alone, the coryza, sore throat, bronchitis or even pneumonia may follow; but if taken early, a dose of Merc. may prevent all such troubles.”
The chilliness is fe/t most generally in the evening and finereases to the night, € not removed by Merc.
It 1s often felt in single parts. Then again it is felt in abscesses, and is the harbinger of pus formation.
5. Salivated tongue with thirst :
There is the characteristic flabby, coated, teeth-indented

104 Synoptic Memorizer of Materia Medica

tongue with foul breath and intense thirst - throat dry and forepart of the tongue ts moist (Ref : Clarke).
Ptyalism *: tenacious, soapy, stringy, profuse, foetid, co-ppery, metallic-tasting saliva.
Tongue : large, flabby, shows imprint of teeth (Chel, Pod.,
Rhus.), painful, with ulcers ; red or white (Ref: Allen’s Key-notes)
Note 1.: Aarely give Merc. if the tongue is dry. (Ref : Gue-rnsey’s Key-notes).
Wote 2. :—Dry tongue but no thirst, Puls., NuxVom., ; —
dry tongue much thirst, Bry, Ars).
6. Offensive discharges, offensive sweat :
Dr. Clarke said the Mercurius patient is offensive; breath excessively foetid (Bapt., Carbo. Acid., Kali.P., Nit-Acid , Sil-)
Sweat : Offensive, mawkish, sweetish.
Profuse sweat accompaning nearly all complaints and sweat does not relieve ; tt may even aggravate, <at night
{Ref : Clarke).
7. Leading tremor :
Dr. Clarke said keynote of Merc. fs tremor. This symptom is SO pronounced and universal that it renders Merc. the best general remedy in paralysis agitans. There is tremor of head, of hands, of tongue. Tremor commencing in the fingers.
It is the tremor of weakness and paralysis and as described by B. Cooper it may attack the heart and cause sudden death on the smallest effort. Short of this there is great tendency to fainting ; extreme exhaustion after a stool. The tremor may become jerkings and even convulsions, extreme rest-lessness.
Dr. Kent said that tremor of the hands, so that the patient can’t lift anything or eat or write
Note 1 : Merc. is a grcat remedy in children with epileptiform fits, twitching and disorderly motions.
Note 2 : The motions of the tongue are disorderly and the child can't talk. Involuntary motion which can be momenta-rily controlled by volition.

GUIDING SYMPTOMS 105

NATRUN MURIATICUM
As Dr. John Henry Clarke said, ““Those who can see nothing but ‘common-salt’ in Natrum Mur. may conclude that they have not ‘the root of the matter’ in them’ thus allow me to impress you Natrum Mur. totality through its common name, i.e ‘Common Salt’’.

41. Consolation < :
Dr. Kent said that consolation aggravated the state of mind—the mefancholy, the fearfulness, sometimes brings on anger. She appears to bid for sympathy and is mad when itis given. The patient prefers to be alone ( Ref : Clarke ).
“Wants to be alone to cry.”’
Nat. Mur. patient A/des their tears for fear of pity and consolation. ( Ref : Blunt.).
2. On coughing urinates :
Involuntary urination when walking, coughing, laughing ( Caust., Puls., Sqifla., Arg.N., Zinc.M., Ferr.P.).
3. Mapped tongue :
Dr Clarke discussed the characteristic tongue of Nat.M. is either a mapped tongue with red islands, or a clean shining tongue with froth along each side There are many charac-teristic symptoms in connection with the tongue ;—hair sensation : numbness and _ stiffness of one side: heavy, embarassing speech.
Nat.M. corresponds to children who are late in talking.

106 Synoptic Memorizer of Materia Medica

The tongue is blistered; sticks to roof of mouth. Dryness of mouth and throat with unquenchable thirst.
Text says tongue like ringworm on sides (Ars, Lach,
Nit.Ac., Tarax. ).

> by lying on right side (—on painful side, Ammon. Carb.,
Bry., Ign., Puls , Calc.C ).
5. On touch hair falls :
The hair falls out when touched, in nursing women (Sep.)
Note. : Face oily, shiny, as if greased ( Plb., Thuja. ).
6. Nervous economy :
The whole nervous economy is in a state of fret and irritation ( Master Kent. ).
Great irritability is the characteristic of Nat.Mur patient; child cross when spoken to.
Crying from slightest cause, gets Into a passion about trifles, especially when consoled with
Hysterical condition of the mind. The lachrymal disposi-tion and hypochondriaca! mood are the key-note of Nat M.
Marked disposition to weep, sad weeping mood without cause (Puls ).
Dreams of robbers in the house, is another pecularity of the mental condition of Nat.M.
Tears stream down the face whenever he caughs (Euph.).
7. Salt craving :
Craving for salt (Cal., Caust., Phos.).
Note : Patient also desires: bitter things, beer, farinaceous foods, sour things, salt, oysters, fish, milk.
8. Aversion and abuse :
Aversion to bread, meat, coffee, tobacco. Master Kent in his Repertory classed Nat.Mur. in first grade under the

GUIDING SYMPTOMS 107

sub-rubric, aversion to bread, China.1, Nat.Mur.?, Con %,
Lyco.*, Nat. S.*, Nit. Ac *, Nux Vom.?, Phos.?, Puls 2,
Sep.*; —aversion to meat, Calc.:, China.*, Graph ?, Mur.Ac.?,
NuxVom.?, Puls 7, Sif +, Sep +, Alumina.*, Carbo.V.2, Lyco.?,
Nat. M.4, Phos.*, Rhus Tox.?.
Ailments from : Bad effects of anger, abuse of excessive use of salt, loss of vital fluid (Carbo.Veg., Staph., China.,) sexual excess, profuse menses.
9. Losing flesh while living well :
Great emaciation, losing flesh while lving well (Abrot., lod, AceticAc , Sanicula , Tuber ,—Ref. Nash); throat and neck of children emaciate rapidly during summer complaints (San.c.).
10. Tremendous emotional and sentimental :
The mentality of Lyco. indicate it’s intellectual side, that of
Nat. Mur. on the emotional and sentimental side.
Kent said Nat. M.is the chronic of Ign. and where the later is too superficial, Nat. Mur. cures.
“Falls in love with the wrong person, and breaks her heart. Is absurdly obsessed by a foolish passion for a married man—falls in love with the coachman, and Nat.M., brings order and sanity.””
NITRIC ACID

108 Synoptic Memorizer of Materia Medica

1. Nervous trembling :
Our Nitric Acid pt has nervous trembling After continued loss of sleep, long lasting anxiety, over-exertion of mind and body from nursing the sick the pt trembles. Dr N.M
Chowdhury said, fe trembles in all his limbs Master Kent also reported of this nervous trembling due to prolonged suffering in broken-down constitution
2. Indigestible things :
Nitric Acid has craving for indigestible things, such as chalk, charcoal, stone-chips etc. ( Alumina.*, Calc *, Calc.Phos.?, others, Cina, Cicutta. Psor. ).
Note. : Great thirstlessness ( Ref : Kent ).
3. Tremendous offensiveness :
Master Kent said, offensiveness is a marked condition of the patient, often putrid odors. Offensive leucorrhoea, catarrh, breath, foetid foot-sweat, strong odors from the body, offen-sive urine Hke that of a horse, —in such cases Nitric Acid find its, similimum, if the other symptoms agrees.
Dr. Clarke said, offensive, thin. excoriating discharges — is the characteristic.
4. Red bloody haemorrhage -
It is one of our leading haemorrhagic remedy ( Arn.?,
Bell.?, Calc.t, Carbo Veg *, China *, Crot. Hor.?, Ham.?, fpec.?,
Lach.?, Melli?, Merc*, Nat. Mur?, Nit. Ac*, NuxVom.?,
Phos.?. Puls.', Sabina.?, Sep.?, Sulph+*, Acon?, Bov.?,

5. trrestible desire to curse and swear :
It 1s our Nitric Acid where /rritab/lity is a marked feature.
Pt has irrestible desire to curse and swear. Master Kent placed it in first grade. (cursing, Anac.*, Nit.Ac.7, Ars.*, Hyos.?,
Lyco *, Nux Vom.?, V.A.? ).
6. Cracks and fissures :
Dr Clarke said, the localities in which the action of Nit.Ac.

GUIDING SYMPTOMS 109

is very strongly marked,—the muco-cutaneous orifices and adjoining parts. Cracks and fissures in these selected parts with splinter like pain, calls for Nit. Ac.. Master Kent said, fissures forms in many places, canthi, corners of the mouth, above the anus ; the skin cracks and all these have the splinter sensation.
7, Adament but unmoved by apolozy :
This is peculiar uncommon symptom that apolozy is in-capable of moving our Nitric. Acid. Dr. N. M. Chowdhury said, head-strong, obstinate, but apology, coaxing, love are equally incapable of moving him.
8. Comes and goes suddenly—pains :
The pains of Nitric Acid are very characteristic.
Pains : i) Cause : On change of temparature or weather.
ii) Onset : Comes suddenly, disappears suddenly
(Bell., Mag Phos }).
iii) Character : Sticking, pricking as from splinters ( Master Kent in his Repertory classed pain : sensation of splinters, Agar.*, Arg Nit.*, Hep.', Nit. Ac.? ). Pains gnowing here and there as from ulcer forming.
Note : Master Kent said, even these pains are aggravated from noise, ar.
9. in affected part splinter :
Sensation of splinter in affected parts, ulcers, pifes, throat ; sensation of a band around head, around the bones (Carb.Ac.,
Sulph. ).
Dr. Kent remarked, sticking in throat like splinter and can be bracketed with (Hepar, Natrum.Mur., Alum., Arg- Nit.,
Dolichos ). Master Kent said, sensation as though a_ splinter felt in inflammed parts, in ulcers and in nerves.
10. Debility :
As in any other acids ; debility and general weakness (Ref :
Kent) is another denoting feature of deep acting Nitric
Acid. Our sagacious Kent has reported, great general weak-ness, feeble reaction — pt- greatly broken-down by long sufferings, finally anaemia and emaciation are marked — Nitric
Acid rescues such cases.

110 Synoptic Memorizer of Materia Medica

NUX VOMICA
Let me impress you the totality of Nux Vomica through the common-name, Le. ‘Poison Nut’.
P=Paralytic conditions (Ref. Kent)
O=Oversensitiveness (mental and physical).
l=Ineffectual desire for stool and urine—the general
cancomitant

1. Paralytic conditions :
Master Kent said, NuxVom. is full of paralytic conditions
The bowels are ina state of excitement but this passes away and the time comes when the faeces remains in the rectum with no warning, this extends to the bladder, so that it be-comes full of urine which can’t be voided, or dribbling of urine; paralysis of the extremities, of the face, of single muscles : with characteristic sticking pains Nux cures such cases, provided totality corroborates.

2. Oversensitiveness :
i) Mentally : Pt. is oversensitrve mentally (Ref : Kent). irritable, touchy. sensitive cenditions, the woman has impulses to destory her husband. to throw her child into the fires, cannot be contradicted—such an aversensitiveness : oversen-sitive to music (Nux Mas.) ; trifling ailments are unbearable, harmless word offends, such a mental oversensitiveness finds its similimum in NuxVom.
ii) Physically . Oversensitive to external impressions, to light, noise, odors, touch. Pt. ig extremely touchy in regard to his food and our Master Kent said oversensitive to
Medicines, oversensitive to stimulants. Tendency to faint from odors, after eating, after every labour pain (Ref. Allen).

GUIDING SYMPTOMS 111

3 Ineffectual desire for stool and urine—the general
concomitant .
‘Frequent and ineffectual desire to defecate but small quantities of faeces at each attempt’—this symptom as
Dr. E. B. Nash said, is pure gold There are a few other remedies that have it, but none so positively and persistently.
It may be coined, that the frequent and in-effectual desire for stool and urine is a general concomitant symptom.
4. Sieep :
Sleep is a characteristic indication of Nux Vom. Dr. N. M.
Chowdhury emphasized that the most important point to remember in this rernedy is that the patients are always worse after a disturbed sleep. There is_ irrestible desire to sleep in the evening, can not keep from falling asleep in the evening while sitting or reading, hours before bed time and consequently pt. is compelled to retire and sleep. He wakes up at about 3 A.M. (Ref. Allen) and then falls into a dreamy sleep early in the morning from which he is hard to arouse, if aroused, he feels tired and weak. Though Dr.N M
Chowdhury reported, pt. find it difficult to sleep again in the early morning, ideas keep on crowding upon them till at last out of sheer exhaustion. he falls asleep again. tried and irritable (— Puls. point of similarity with Nux Vom., wide awake in the evening, does not want to go to bed.).
5. Oversensitive to cold :
Dr. £. B. Nash said, chilliness of Nux Vom. is a character-istic. Great tendency to take cold and aversion or repug-nance to cold air. Pt. is compelled to close the doors and windows and cover-up the body. Chilly on feast movement, from being uncovered, must be covered from head to feet in every stage of fever. Master Kent said, over-sensitive to open air, to. a draft of air always chilly. always taking coid, cold air aggravates ( Master Kent in his Repertory graded Nux Vom. in first grade under the sub-rubric, cold air aggravates, Ars.?,
Baryta-1, Calc.C.?, Caust.4, Dulc.?, Hell-4. Hep.*, Lyco.?,
N.V.2, Rhus Tox.?, Psor.?, Rumex.?, Sep.?, Sil-7. } (—cold air ameliorates fod.1, Lyco.?, Puls.?.) ¢( Tendency to take cold,

Acon.*, Baryta-?, Bry.1, Calc. Phos.?, Chamo.+, Dulc.2, Hep.*,
Lyco.*, Merc.?, Nat. Mur.?, Nit. Ac.?, Nux Vom.?, Psor.',
Rumex.?+, Sil-? ).
Note : Catarrh ameliorates in cold air and aggravates in warm room.
6. Nash’s sum-up :
Dr. E. B. Nash aptly sum-up the essence of Nux Vom. through sens/tiveness, mervousness and chilliness—three general characteristic of Nux Vom.
7. Nervous temperament :
Dr. Nash said Nux. Vom. bears nervous temperament and can be classed with Chamo., Ign., Staph. Nervous, Hyper-impressionable, thin. spare subjects (Ref. Farrington). In this temperamental concern we must know the verdict of our immortal Master Samuel Hahnemann, that prodigious perso-nality has reported. “-Nux is chiefly successful with persons of an ardent character. of an irritable. impatient temperament. disposed to anger, spite or deception.”
8. Universal antidote :
Our Nux Vom. is one of the best remedies with which to commence treatment of cases that have been drugged by mixtures, bitters, vegetable pills, nostrum or quack remedies, esp., aromatic or hot medicines Master Kent said, over-drugged by the ofd-schoo!,—Nux Vom. acts as an universa!
antidote.
Master Kent said when a patient comes from the old school and bad prescribing. having had stimulants and tonics to brace him up. wine. and stiumulants of all sorts, it is sometimes impossible to get reliable symptoms; to get the pt. settled down, we give Nuxas an antidote.
Note : Dr. £. Nash said, it would be true if said that Nux
Vomica will often benifit such cases. The facts is the use of such drugs, aromatics, pills etc. has brought about a condition that, it will benifit those cases in which that stimulates the symptoms produced in the provings of Nux Vomica, or in cases to which it is, homoeopathic, and no others.

GUIDING SYMPTOMS 113

9. Trembling :
Master Kent said trembling of parts,—spasm is another characteristic of NuxVom. Dr. E. B. Nash also emphasized that spasm is a characteristic features spasm from simple twitchings to clonic form : convulsions with consciousness-characterizes the remedy.
Dr. Harvey Farrington said, Nux. produces twitching and jerking of muscles in all parts of the body. strabismus, cramps
in the extremities ; the convulsions may at times characterized by protruding eyes, blueness of the lips, tossing and rolling about. sudden drawing up of the limbs and thursting them out again.
PHOSPHORUS

H = Haemorrhage.

The perspiration of Phos.. is somewhat peculiar, it has the odor of sulphur. Though in Kents’ Repertory, Master Kent graded this feature in third grade, yet this peculiar type of perspiration has been considered as a leading indication by vario s authorities.
(—perspiration has the odor of cheese, Hep.?, —like spoiled egg, Sulph.? ; — foetid, Hep.*, — honey like, Thuja.* ;

2. Haemorrhage :
Dr. John Henry Clarke said it corresponds to haemorrhagic diathesis. Dr. E. B. Nash said, profuse and persistent bleeding, even from small wounds and turnours. Master Kent said, haemorrhage from the stomach, from the bladder, from the uterus and from uleerations. Small wounds bleeds much, bright red blood.
Dr. Allen reported, frequent and profuse blood, pouring out freely and then ceasing for a time.
Master Kent rightly denoted that Phos. has haemorrhagic constitution. Master Kent in his masterly Repertorial work classed that, “b/ood does not coaguiate’’, Lach.*, Nit. Ac.?,
Phos.?, Apis.*, Carbo Veg #, Crot. Hor®, Elaps.?, Kali Ph.?,
Secale.?.

Oversensitiveness of all the senses, to external impressions, light, noise, touch, odor. Master Kent said, slight causes lead to exhaustion of either body or mind; trembling through-out the body from slight causes. Master Kent in his Reper-tory graded Phos. in first grade under the both rubrics, sansitive externally as well as internally. ( —sensitiveness,
externally, Apis., Arn., Bell... China., Lach., Nux Vom., Phos.,
Puls., Silt, Spig., Staph. ; —internally, Canth., Hep., Lach.,
Nat. Mur. Phos., Sil. ).
4. Sinking sensation :
A weak, empty, a//-gone sensation in head, chest, stomach and entire abdamen. Or. Clarke reported that the sinking, faint feeling of Phos. is felt in the whole abdominal cavity, also in head, chest and stomach. Master Kent in his Repertory classed emptiness in abdomen, Arg.N.*, Cocc.4, Phos.?,
Podo.?, Puls.*, Sep.4, Stannum.*, Sulp.Ac.*, Tab?. ; —hungry fesling, gonengss, faintriess, weak-feeling. emptiness in sto-mach, Ant.C.?, tgn.*, Merc.?, Nux Vom.*, Phas.*, Podo.4,
Puls.*, Sep.*, Sulph.*, V.A.4, Zine,* 7 (—at 11 A.M., Sulph 3,
Nat. C.2, Phos.*, Zinc.*; —not relieved by eating, Cina?, ign.?, Lyca.*, Lach.?, Phos.*, V.A.7.).

GUIDING SYMPTOMS 115

5. Pain :
Dr. Allen remarked, pain : acute, esp. in the chest, aggra-vation from pressure, even slight, and lying on feft side; excited by slightest chill ; open air intolerable. Master Kent said, tearing, drawing, burning pains throughout the body, pt. wants to be rubbed, and better after sleep.
6. Heat running up the back — burning :
Dr. John Henry Clarke said, feeling of intense heat running up the back is a leading characteristic, and he has clearly emphasized that mo other remedy has exactly this symptam. in this regard it is to note that Phos. is one of the trio of
Nash’s burners ( others, Ars. Alb. and Sulph. ). Burning, in spots, along the spine, between the scapulae, or of palms, in chest and lungs, of every organ or tissues of tre body. generally in diseases of nervous system. Dr. Clarke said, burning palms, can t bear to have the hands covered, flushes of heat begining in hands and spread to face. Master Kent also reported of this burning ; burning in the brain, in the skin, in various parts. Dr. E. B. Nash said, t#ere fs no organ or tissue in which the burning may not be found, trom the outer skin to the innermost surface of every tract or parenchyma.
7. Opposite of Chelidonium Le. craves coldest drink :
Our Phos craves coldest drink in Materia Medica (—hotest drink, almost boiling, Cheli.). Dr. Clarke said, Phos. has burning thirst for cold water, cold water relieves, but as soon as it becomes warm in the stomach it is vomited.
Dr. Clarke also emphasized that desire for cold foods and preference of cold meat is very characteristic of Phos., and the cold food like the cold drink. may be vomited as soon as it becomes warm in the stomach. Desires cold drinks,
Acon.?, Ars.*, Bry.*, Chamo.*, China.*, Cina.*, Merc.1, Phos.1,
V.A,*, —-cold food, Phos.?, Puls.*, Ant Tart.*, Lyco.*, Sil.?,
Thuja.?, V.A.? ) ( Ref. Kent’s Repertory ).
8. Restless :
Phos. is one of our restless remedies; restless, fidgety ; moves continually, cannot sit or stand-still a moment,
{ — Nash’s trio of restless medicines, Acon., Ars.Alb., Rhus

Tox. : —rheumatic pain drive him out of bed at night and compels him to walk about, Chamo., Rhus Tox. ; —
at night unable to get an easy position or lie still a moment.
Caust., Eup., RhusTox. ; —fidgety while sitting at work,
Graph. ; —fidgety feeling in the feet or lower extremities, must move them continuously, Zincum. ).
9. Un-scommon peculiar indications :
There are some uncommon peculiar indications, which characterizes the medicine, viz :
i) Nausea from placing hands in warm water; though a chilly pt.
ii) During pregnancy ; unable to drink water ; sight of it causes vomiting ; must close her eyes while bathing.
10. Stoop-shouldered, slender persons :
Dr. Allen reported, young, tall, slender persons of sanguine, sensitive temperament, who grow too rapidly, are inclined to stoop—(Cwalk stooped, Sulph.). Dr. Clarke said, slender, narrow-chested, slim and disposed to stoop, are our Phos. patients.
PULSATILLA
Doctor | a tearful blonde has come to your chamber, while
narrating her symptoms breaks into tears; your diagnosis-——
Pulsatilia 200/4 Doses. Thus allow me to impress you the
Puisatilla totality through ‘PULS. 2C/4D.’
P-==Pains.
U-Uncommon peculiar thirstless.
L_==Lachrymal.

4. Pain:
The pains are changeable and erratic. Character of the

GUIDING SYMPTOMS 117

pain is drawing, tearing. They come and go and keep on changing their locations. Pains rapidly shifted from one part to another (Kali Bi., Lac C, Mang. Ac.). As Master Hering said, “Wandering pain shifts rapidly from one part to another, also with swelling and redness of joints’. According to Dr.
Clarke, “The wandering pains of Puls. are generally distensive again suggesting congested vessels , and the headaches are congestive ; <.on stooping forward ;>by tightly bandaging.
Dr. N. M. Chowdhury said, “another peculiarity of the pain is that it is almost accompanied by chills,—the severity of the chills being measured by the intensity of the pain. The association of these two symptoms has always been for us a great index and it has scarcely ever disappointed us”.
Pains ; ‘appears suddenly, leave gradually or tension much increases until very acute and then “lets up with a snap’’; on first motion (Rhus.) (Ref. Allen). Pain is relieved by pressure and lying on affected side and by cold application. Pain is aggravated by hot application and lying on painless side.
Master Kent says, ““Pulsatilla has wandering pains; rheuma-tism goes from joint to joint, jumps around here and there; neuralgic pain fly from place to place.”
Thus let us sum up :
i) Onset : Pain appears suddenly leaves gradually
or vis-a-vis.
li) Character : Pain rapidly shifting from one part to
another (Kali. Bi., Kali. S., Lac. Can.,
Mag. P., Phyto.).
iit) Modality : Pain is relieved by pressure and lying
on affected side (Am. C., Bry.).
iv) Concomitant : Pain is accompanied by chilliness,
greater the pain greater the chilliness.
(—pain accompanied by profuse swe-ating, Chamo.,— with fainting, Hepar. ;:
—with frequent micturition, Thuja. ;
—with delirium, Veratrum.) (Ref. Nash.).
2, Uncommon peculiar thirstlessness :
Thirstlessness is one of the index of Puls., it persists nearly

118 Synoptic Memorizer of Materia Medica

in ali complaints. As Master Kent says, “a striking feature of the Pulsatilla patient is that. he mever wants wafer. But exception in high fevers,—there may be some thirst” (Ref. Dr.

Kent). ‘‘Weeps about everything 7 can hardly give her symptoms on account of weeping “ (Ref. Dr. Hering). Crying all the time but crying makes her worse (Nat.Mur., Sep., Stannum.) (Ref. Allen), yet consolation amel/orates. Dr. N. M. Choudhury said, ‘this tendency to weep is, ! consider, the most important feature of the Pulsatifla patient.”
4. Sleep :
“Wide awake in the evening. does not want to go to bed ; first sleep restless, sound asleep when it is time to get up: awakes languid, unfreshed."" (Ref. Dr. Allen).
Patient sleeps on the back with hands over the head.
Can not sleep on the left side as it increases the palpitation and suffocation. Late falling asleep; sleeplessness on account of flushes of heat. (Ref. Dr. Kent.) He moves about in his sleep. Sleeplessness from ebullition of blood. He starts up in fright in his sleep. Chattering in his sleep.
Constant sleepiness and comatose sleep. with agitation and disquieting fancies, day or night. Great tendency to sleep during.the day, principally in evening or afternoon.

During sleep, chattering, talking, delirium, convulsive move-ments of mouth, eyes. limbs, —cries and moans, night-mare; starts from fright. (Ref : Dr: Clarke‘’s Dictionary
Vol. IE).
5. Changeableness:
Changeableness is another feature of the Pulsatilla. This
changeableness is a general characteristic of this remedy
and we find it is manifested in all its symptoms.
This is the characteristic changeableness of Pulsatilla,
manifested in the mental as well as in physical sphere.
A) Changeableness in mental sphere :
While she is mild, gentle and tearful, yet she is remarkably irritable, not in the sense of pugnacity, but easily irritated, extremely touchy, always feels slighted or fears she will be slighted ; sensible to every social influence. ( Ref. Kent’s lecture. )}; Dr. Nash said, “the patient is now /rritable, then tearful again; or mild and pleasant, but even with the irritableness.”
B) Changeableness in physical sphere :
“No two chills, no two stools, 70 two attacks are alike: very well one hour, very miserable the next ; apparently con-tradictory”’ ( Ref : Allen.)
Pains shifts rapidly from one part to another. A striking feature of the bowel symptom, it is continually changing ; in summer complaints, when Puls. is the indicated remedy, there will be hardly two stools are alike. This is the characteristic of Puls. in general ; the pains wander ; complaints change by metastasis ; the patient is ever twice alike. Diarrhoea alter-nates with constipation:—menstrual flow stops and_ starts, intermits and changes. [n the patient, you never know what you will find the next. Now dyseneric stool, next stools may be diarrhoeic. Patient is scarcely ever twice alike. (Ref. Dr.
Kent's lecture).
Dr. Nash said, ‘Puls. will often clear up those cases which have no “head or tail’’ to thern ; in which the symptoms are always changing and contradicting”.

Alternate pale and redness of face. When one set of symp-toms comes and another vanished (Ref. Dr. Clarke).
6. Chilliness :
Just by only the meaning of the chilliness, it seems that ordinarily it is a common symptom; but this chilliness becomes highly characteristic of Puls. ; due to its constant association with the other complaints and modalities effec-ting it. As because we know that severity of the chills being
measured by the intensity of the disease.
Chilliness from emotional excitement ; external chilliness and internal heat with diarrhoea—after fright ; anxiety with shivering ; chattering of the teeth and hot flushes; in short, chilliness in a warm room; even when warmly clad, passing off in the open air. (Ref. Harvey Farrington, M.D,)
The Puls. pt. is chilly, but at the same time there is extre-me aversion to heat. The three characters,—“chilly; aggrava-ted by warmth ; thirstless ;’ serve to define the fever of Puls.
in what-ever form it may be met,—measfes, mumps, tvphoid, bilious, catarrhal, intermittent, rheumatic etc. The chilliness
may be one sided, and associated with numbness, it may be flitting, in spots now here, now there. (Ref. Clarke).
‘Chilliness | one look up Puls, as one of the “warm remedies”. But it has produced and cured chilliness, as we go through its black letter symptoms among other things, it has chilliness in a warm room’. (Ref. Dr. Tyler.)
7. Derangement :
Derangement at puberty, all the complaints are caused by derangement at pubertal age. Has never been well since that time. First sarious derangement of health is referred to the age of puberty, “never been well since,’’—anaemia. bronchitis, phthisis’. (Ref. Dr. Clarke).
8. Desire :
“Desire for sour, refreshing things,” often desires things he can not digest ; lemonade, cheese, pungent things, highly-seasoned things, juicy things, (“aversion to: meat, butter, fatty food, pork, bread, milk, smoking’). Craves ice-GUIDING SYMPTOMS 121

him worse ; craves things which makes him sick. This is
mot uncommon. The whisky drinker craves liquor, yet knows it will kill him. So in Pulsatila with regard to pastries.
Craves butter cakes, with maple syrup, yet knows they will be vomited. Craves highly spiced sausage, yet averse to pork alone ( Ref. Master Kent }
9. Discharge:
The discharges from all the mucous membranes are thick bland, greenish yellow.
But Dr Kent savs, leucorrhoea may be scmetimes acrid and excoriating, causing rawness of the part.
The discharges are also non-irritating : seldom are they thin and watery, sometimes feucorrhoea becomes acrid, causing rawness & biting of the vagina ( Ref. Harvey Farrington ).
Discharges are often offensive, sometimes bloody, watery, but even then mingled with yellow green purulent fluid (Ref. Dr. Kent).
10. Diarrhoea:
Only or usually at night, watery, greenish yellow, very changeable ; soon as they eat; from fruit, cold food or drinks, /ce-creams (Ref. Allen); diarrhoea, changeable, stools preceded by rumbling and cutting in the abdomen; worse at night; from fruit or ice-cream (Ref. Dr. Harvey

CHAPTER—4

PHYSIOLOGICAL ACTIONS
Phystological action means the action produced by the drug in its crude form (crude medicinal extract) and in mas-sive dose’ Intrue sense the term or etymology——‘massive dose’ is apparently vague, as because there are lethal dose, maximal permissible dose, dosis tolerata or tolerance dose etc.

Thus as Stedman‘s medica! dictionary explicits the ety-mology—‘physiologic’, which denotes the action of a drug when given to a healthy person, as distinguished from its therepeutic action.

Dr. Stuart Close in his book “‘The genius of Homoeo-pathy—Homoeopathic Philosophy’’—clearly elucidated that,
‘The physiological action of a drug is notits therepeutic or curative action It is exactly the opposite of a curative action and is never employed in homoeopathic practice for there-peutic purposes. The use of the word ‘Physiological’ in conneetion with drug action and drug dosage tends to mis-lead the unwary and just:fy the use of measures which would otherwise be regarded as illegitimate. CHAPTER-—9
RELATIONSHIP OF REMEDIES
ANTIDOTE : Stedman’s Medica! dictionary reveals that anti=against ; dotos=whatis given; ie, an agent that neutralizes a poison or counteracts its effccts
Dr. E, A, Farrington elucidated that, there are drugs, which antidote each other Your pt. may be too susceptible to the action of the remedy, and you require to modify its effects, viz, Farrington explained a case where he prescribed Nux Vom. for a cold. It has relieved the pt. of his cold, but he became almost crazy with headache ; ic. due to the fact that he had and excess of Nux Vomica, hence Farrington prescribed
Coffea, and in ten minutes the headache was better This was done by simply modifying the effects of Nux
RELATIONSHIP

Vomica ; as Coffea counteracted with it ; antidoted the bad effects.
COMPLEMENTARY : The word comes from complemention ie, which completes. -The term com-plement means that, one drug completes the cure which the other begins ; —but the former drug was unable to terminate in cure, which the latter does; thus these two drugs are said to be complementary drugs, — viz.,
OF REMEDIES

Belladonna and Calearea Dr. Clarke said, when a remedy has done all that it can, ima case, then another remedy is likely to follow up and complete its action, where both are related to the case,—as Bryonia and
Rhus Tox. are complementary drugs.
Dr. Boenninghausen said, some remedies are in harmony with others, the most similar one, as a rule are complementary, they antidotes each other's bad effects, follow each other well, and often make-up for the
Reln.

deficiencies of the others. Others with a lesser degree of similarity may be used at a greater interval of time and finish up the work started by the other remedies.
I

CONCORDANT : The drugs which present marked similarities in action, though dissimilar in origin.
Drugs holds a concordant relation may follow each other well,— viz , Bryonia and Alumina.
Reln.
INIMICAL : There are drugs which have relation of enmity amongst them. They may resembling
each other apparantly, will not follow one another with any satisfaction ; they seem to mix-up the case (Ref.
Farrington)— it can also be said that they do harmful effects if followed, or spoils the action of the former,—
such drugs are said to be inimical between them, —viz., Apis Mel. and Rhus Tox.

Usually there is insidious onset, or when acute
diseases assume a typhoid form

3. Symptoms at onset
i) Rhus Tox may be indicated in any and every

and continuous type of fevers.

by chill with great thirst and dryness of ton-gue, mouth and throat.

at the onset there ts diarrnoea witn beginning

the evening and accompanied by paroxysms
of pain and other accessory symptoms
v) Internal shivering with external heat and
vice-versa.
vi) Fever inthe evening; first shivering, then
heat and thirst (and perspiration); accom-panied and followed by cutting pain and

External coldness atong the skin but does
